This is really missing the underlying problem. Migrant labor in the not so distant future will be undercut by increased automation. Are we then going to try to pass laws that companies aren't allowed to use technology to increase their efficiency and cut costs? No, that's ridiculous. Instead at some point we need to start considering that the long term view for an economic system based around widescale employment simply does not exist. It's not sustainable.

It's nothing about the population, or immigrants or whatever. It's simple productivity increases. In the 50s we may have needed 60 people working to generate the commodities for 100 people. With modern technology those same 60 people can now generate the commodities for 500 people. It doesn't matter if you have a population of a billion or a million, it's a matter of productivity which scales with population whichever way you go.

We only get upset about things like this because it puts a face to the problem, and a foreign face at that. But that face is little more than a red herring. In total there are less than 150k H1-B visas given out each year. To think that is having some major impact on a country of 300 million is just silly. The only reason it's contentious is because it's finally having something to point your finger at. There are just fewer and fewer desirable jobs and seeing any of them go to 'outsiders' is just salting the wound.

150K jobs per year is still a hell of a lot. And it will have knock-on effects - if your third-party IT support goes down the pan, your company will suffer too.

This isn't so much "foreigners coming to take our jobs" as "companies are abusing the law to recruit cheap foreigners".
